comparison: Both evaluations strongly agree on GDA-2 dynamics and RpoS mechanism. They share 11 claims (C54-C56, C58, C62-C63, C65, C67-C70) with 78.6% overlap. OpenEval emphasizes mutual exclusivity and fitness effects, while peer review highlights the competitive displacement aspect. Both accept the mechanistic connection to RpoS activity.

Both evaluations agree on divergent evolutionary trajectories and maintenance of unstable DHFR mutants through duplication. They share 12 claims (C7, C82-C88, C91-C93, C95) with 75% overlap. OpenEval provides detailed mechanistic reasoning about promoter mutations, while peer review emphasizes compensation for proteolytic instability. Both affirm the epistatic interactions.

Both evaluations agree on general principles of GDA dynamics and stability. They share synthesis claims C106-C108 with 75% overlap. OpenEval synthesizes temporal dynamics across all experiments, while peer review characterizes this as 'important and convincing proof of principle.' Both accept GDA instability and transient nature.

Both evaluations agree on variable expression and fitness costs of duplications. They share claims C43-C47 with 71.4% overlap. OpenEval emphasizes RNA-seq data and competition assays showing costs comparable to mgrB inactivation, while peer review accepts the expression and fitness data as rigorous without specific critique.

Both evaluations agree on the central mechanistic conclusion linking proteostasis to gene dosage evolution. They share synthesis claims C8-C9, C105, C110, C112 with 50% overlap. OpenEval integrates multiple experimental observations, while peer review affirms this as 'rigorous and convincingly support the conclusions' regarding proteolytic stability as a determinant.

Both evaluations agree on GDA mutations and lon-knockout effects. They share 6 claims (C2-C4, C26, C31-C32) with 40% overlap. OpenEval groups folA duplication evidence (C38-C42) separately, while peer review includes lon stimulation claims (C33-C34) and initial characterization (C27, C30). Both affirm the clarity of lon's role in stimulating GDA.

Both evaluations agree on temporal dynamics of GDA loss and point mutation acquisition. They share 6 claims (C6, C71-C73, C75-C76) with 31.6% overlap. OpenEval emphasizes competition assays (C78-C81) showing point mutants outcompete GDA mutants, while peer review groups these with instability claims (C48-C51) and identifies this as a 'key finding.'

Both evaluations address GDA instability in drug-free conditions. They share 5 claims (C5, C48-C51) with 29.4% overlap. OpenEval focuses on rapid loss of duplications with IC50 and sequencing data, while peer review groups these with longer-term displacement dynamics (C70-C76, C109). Both accept the inherent instability of GDA mutations.

Both evaluations address epistatic interactions and proteolytic stability. They share 4 claims (C96-C97, C103-C104) with 28.6% overlap. OpenEval emphasizes genotype-dependent effects through IC50 measurements, while peer review integrates this with broader mechanistic conclusions (C8-C9, C105, C110, C112). Both affirm lon-dependent epistasis.

Both evaluations address lon-knockout effects but with different emphases. They share 2 claims (C33-C34) with 15.4% overlap. OpenEval focuses on transposase stability and mechanistic inference, while peer review groups these with broader GDA emergence evidence (C2-C4, C26-C27, C30-C32). Both support increased GDA frequency in lon-knockout.

Minimal overlap with 2 shared claims (C27, C30) at 14.3%. OpenEval focuses on initial characterization of WTMPR and LTMPR isolates with pitA validation (C24-C25, C28-C29), while peer review groups these with broader GDA emergence findings. Both accept the characterization data as thorough.

Minimal overlap with 2 shared claims (C41-C42) at 12.5%. Both accept the protein and transcript measurements supporting folA duplication effects.
